narrative:
Every road out of the Realm begins with a reason to leave. Yours is not the same as anyone else's.

Before the Salt Road, before the failing fields, before the first person asks what you will sacrifice for a stranger—there is the life that taught you how to answer.

narrative:
You learned the road does not ask who your parents were. It asks who keeps walking after the fire goes out, after the last innkeeper says no, after a friend takes the easier path without you.

You still carry a button from the coat of the person who taught you that lesson. The metal has been rubbed smooth by bad weather and worse nights. You have never decided whether keeping it is loyalty or cowardice.

At the edge of another nameless village, a yellowed field catches your eye. You know the look of a place beginning to run out of chances.

choices.label: Follow the road toward the village

effects.run_history: Left the road behind long enough to answer a village's trouble

narrative:
Your hands remember seed grain, wet earth, and the terrible arithmetic of a pantry in late winter. You did not leave home because ordinary life was beneath you. You left because ordinary people deserve someone who comes back when trouble starts.

The messenger's boots leave small crescents of mud across your floor. They apologize for it twice. You remember doing the same thing when you were young and afraid that making a mess was worse than bringing bad news.

A messenger brings word of sick fields on the next road over. You are already packing before the sentence ends.

narrative:
At court, people kneel in perfect rows and call obedience peace. You watched your father receive a petition from hungry farmers without ever meeting their eyes. Later, a servant gathered the dropped wax seals as though the petition had been a spill.

That night, you take the kitchen stair instead of the grand door. A scullery girl recognizes you and says nothing. You leave a silver crown beside her bucket; she leaves it there until you are gone.

You ride out in a plain cloak with your signet hidden against your palm. If House Aldric is worth defending, you decide, it must survive the truth of its own roads.

effects.run_history: Left the Aldric court to see the realm's hunger firsthand

narrative:
You have watched kingdoms call their disasters unprecedented, then repeat the same old mistake with newer banners. The wind from the Hollow Reaches carries a dry, wrong taste—the memory of a blight your people named long before Aldric's line.

At the boundary stone, a young human couple has tied red thread around a dead branch for luck. You do not tell them the old name for the sickness. Some knowledge is a blade; some is only weight.

You take your bow from its case. Old knowledge is only wisdom if it is used before the graveyard fills.

narrative:
The mountain taught you that a crack ignored becomes a collapse. When a Salt Road miller sends for iron braces and says the grain is spoiling before it can be ground, you hear the crack beneath his words.

Before leaving, you tap the lintel of your workshop three times. Your mother taught you the habit, then spent forty years pretending it was not a superstition. The stone is cold beneath your knuckles.

You shoulder your tools. Stone, wood, and people all fail faster when no one bothers to shore them up.

choices.label: Take the road with your tools

effects.run_history: Set out to answer a miller's call for help

narrative:
A hundred years ago, you watched a king call famine a regrettable necessity. Tonight the same fear beats through a roadside inn: too many people counting too few sacks of grain.

A child at the next table is saving the soft middle of a roll for a sibling who is not present. You look away before anyone notices you have noticed. Some hungers make witnesses feel like thieves.

Hunger recognizes hunger. You pull your hood lower and leave before the first frightened heart can decide what you are.

effects.run_history: Followed the first signs of famine from a roadside inn

narrative:
Your old company taught you to read an ambush from a bent bird and a silent hedge. They also taught you what happens when officers count rations before names.

You still wake expecting the cook's ladle to hit the iron pot three times: once for breakfast, once for orders, once for whoever would not eat. No pot rings here. Your body hears it anyway.

When you hear that a village granary is nearly empty, you turn toward it. Maybe you can keep one hungry crowd from becoming the kind of job your old captain would take for coin.

narrative:
Rain comes at dusk and turns the Salt Road into a ribbon of black mud. Beneath the awning of a shuttered smithy, an old man is feeding kindling into a fire too small for the weather. A patched cart waits beside him, one wheel wrapped in rope.

He notices you noticing it.

@Hendrik: Don't stare at the wheel like that. It's held on through two winters and one wedding. That's more than I can say for most promises.

He offers you the dry half of the awning without asking your name.
